item.caption:
If you’re not capable of losing, you’re not qualified to win.

Stoic philosopher Epictetus makes the case that before undertaking anything, we need to understand what we’re getting ourselves into, including what will be required of us and the possible consequences.

He uses the example of someone wanting to compete in the Olympic Games. Before pursuing the glory of winning, they need to consider the discipline, sacrifice, and physical punishment that come with training and competing. And after all that preparation and effort, they may still lose.

That’s part of what they signed up for. And the same should be expected of anyone running for public office. 

Losing isn’t an unforeseen consequence of an election. If we’re going to entrust someone with the responsibility of leading, we have every right to expect them to accept the full terms of that undertaking, not just the outcome they hope to achieve.

That doesn’t mean legitimate questions about election results shouldn’t be investigated. But questioning an outcome and refusing to accept the possibility of losing are two very different things.

There’s another challenge for those running for office, the danger of allowing the position to become part of your identity.

When someone’s sense of who they are becomes tied to the title they hold, the authority they have, or the recognition that comes with it, losing threatens far more than their position. It threatens their sense of self. The more someone has invested their identity in holding that office, the more their ego has to lose.

A position is something you may earn, hold, and eventually lose. It should never become the foundation of who you are.

Our egos can become remarkably creative and sneaky, twisting even a loss into further proof that we were right all along.

Which is what brings us to the words Marcus Aurelius wrote 2,000 years ago: 
“Vanity is terrifyingly good at derailing rational thought.” 
…….

item.caption:
🗳️ I VOTED! HAVE YOU? 🇺🇸

You may not be interested in politics, but politics is certainly involved in your everyday life!

Think about it. The quality of education our children receive, the cost of groceries, access to healthcare, housing affordability, and even the safety of our communities are all influenced by decisions made in government.

As a mother, teacher, and wellness advocate, I see how public policies affect real families every day.

Voting isn't just about choosing leaders. It's about participating in decisions that shape our lives and the future our children will inherit.

VOTE, OR ELSE… others will make those decisions without your input!

Your voice matters. Your participation matters. And civic responsibility doesn't end when the polls close.

🗳️ Let's talk!

1. Have you voted yet?
2. Which issue matters most to you right now: education, healthcare, food prices, or housing?
3. Do you believe we take our civic responsibilities seriously enough?

Stay informed. Get involved. Make your voice count! ❤️

#IVoted #YourVoiceMatters #CivicEngagement #ElectionDay
